explanations.explanation: Eight it is. Josiah, king of Judah, takes the throne at eight and reigns in Jerusalem thirty-one years. I know grown adults who can't stick with a gym membership for thirty-one days. This boy stuck with a kingdom.

Twelve is in this story, but it's a different number. The twelfth year of his reign is when Josiah begins cleansing Judah and Jerusalem. Josiah, king of Judah, was eight when he became king, so you grabbed a real number and hung it on the wrong peg. Happens to me with oven timers all the time.

Sixteen sounds like a sensible age for a king, I'll give you that. But the text says Josiah, king of Judah, was eight years old when he became king. He reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years. Eight is the number that makes you read the verse twice.

explanations.answer: He does what's right in the LORD's eyes
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Josiah did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in the ways of his father David. David was Israel's great king. The text adds that Josiah did not turn aside to the right or to the left. A straight line, friend. I can't even cut a straight line through a cookie sheet.

explanations.answer: He does evil in the LORD's eyes
explanations.explanation: Not this king. The text says Josiah did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. He walked in the ways of his father David, Israel's great king, and did not turn aside to the right or to the left. I can see why a kid king might sound risky, but this one is a good surprise.

explanations.answer: He follows whatever his advisers say
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions advisers steering him here. What it does say is that Josiah did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. He walked in the ways of his father David and did not turn aside to the right or to the left. I won't add a crowd of advisers to the story that the verse doesn't give us.

True. In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still young, Josiah began to seek the God of his father David. Josiah, king of Judah, was young, and he went looking for God anyway. Nobody had to drag him to the kitchen, so to speak.

It's actually true. The text says that in the eighth year of his reign, while he was still young, Josiah began to seek the God of his father David. Josiah was king of Judah, and David was Israel's great king. Easy one to second-guess when you're looking for a trap, friend.

Right on target. In his twelfth year Josiah began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images. That's a long list, and he works through it. Some folks can't even clear out their junk drawer, and I would know.

No soldiers on this list. The text says Josiah began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images. The cleanup is about those things, not armies. Good guess if you were picturing a big showdown, but this is a different kind of cleanup.

The merchants stay put in this passage. What Josiah clears out is the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images. The text says he began that cleansing in his twelfth year. Your market stalls are safe, friend.

The text says the opposite. The altars of the Baals were torn down in his presence. Josiah, king of Judah, was right there for it. Not watching from a balcony with his feet up, either. Hands-on kings are rare, and this one is one.
False is right. The text says the altars of the Baals were torn down in his presence. Josiah, king of Judah, was there when it happened. He wasn't hiding back at the palace waiting for a report.

Graves is the word. Josiah shattered the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images, crushed them to dust, and scattered them over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. It's a heavy moment, so I'll just leave it right there.

Fields sounds reasonable, but that's not what the verse says. The text says the dust was scattered over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. Josiah, king of Judah, had shattered the idols and crushed them to dust first. It's a heavy part of the story, so I'll keep it simple.

No rivers in this verse. The text says Josiah crushed the idols to dust and scattered it over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. He is Josiah, king of Judah. It's a heavy detail, so let's just note it and keep moving.

Not quite. Josiah kept going after Judah and Jerusalem were cleansed. The text says he did the same in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali, and in the ruins around them. This king didn't stop at the first batch, friend.

False is right. After Judah and Jerusalem were cleansed, Josiah did the same in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali. He worked in the ruins around them too. This job had a long list, and he kept on until the work was done.

Home it is. After tearing down the altars and Asherah poles throughout the land of Israel, the text says he returned to Jerusalem. That's the city where he reigned. A long road trip, and he heads home to the capital.
Damascus never comes up in this passage. The text says that after the cleansing throughout the land of Israel, Josiah returned to Jerusalem. That's where he reigned. No detour, friend.

Hebron isn't on this route. The text says Josiah returned to Jerusalem after tearing down the altars and Asherah poles throughout the land of Israel. Josiah was king of Judah, and Jerusalem was where he reigned. Easy to pick another city name when you're guessing, but this verse names the one.

explanations.answer: Repair the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the assignment. Josiah sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God. The text says this was in order to cleanse the land and the temple. Three men, one big repair job.

A wall rebuild is a fine project, but it's not this one. The text says Josiah sent Shaphan, Maaseiah and Joah to repair the house of the LORD his God. Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, had a temple to take care of.

explanations.answer: Count the fighting men of Judah
explanations.explanation: No head count here. The text says Josiah sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God. The job was a repair crew, not a roll call. Good thing, because I'd lose count around the fourth batch.

The text says more than that. The Levites who guarded the doors collected the money from the people of Manasseh and Ephraim, from all the remnant of Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from the people of Jerusalem. Jerusalem was one group out of several. A whole crowd gave.

False is right. The Levites who guarded the doors collected the money from the people of Manasseh and Ephraim, from all the remnant of Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from the people of Jerusalem. Jerusalem was just one of the groups. That's a lot of folks giving to one house.

That's the next stop for the money. The three men gave it to Hilkiah the high priest, and then it was put into the hands of those supervising the work in the house of the LORD. They in turn gave it to the workmen restoring and repairing the house. The money moves down the line to where the work is.

The text doesn't send it there. After the three men gave the money to Hilkiah the high priest, it was put into the hands of those supervising the work in the house of the LORD. They then gave it to the workmen restoring and repairing the house. The money headed for the work, not a vault.

Close, because a priest is in the story. The money went to Hilkiah the high priest first. After that it was put into the hands of those supervising the work in the house of the LORD, and they gave it to the workmen restoring and repairing the house. The text doesn't send it to priests' families.

Dressed stone is right. The text says they gave money to the carpenters and builders to buy dressed stone, as well as timbers for couplings and beams for the buildings. That's solid building material for a worn-down house. Repairs aren't glamorous, but I love them.

Fine linen sounds fancy, but it isn't in this verse. The text says the carpenters and builders got money to buy dressed stone, as well as timbers for couplings and beams for the buildings. This was a repair job with real building materials.

No gold leaf in this verse. The money went to the carpenters and builders to buy dressed stone, as well as timbers for couplings and beams for the buildings. These were the buildings the kings of Judah had allowed to deteriorate. The shopping list was stone and wood.
True. The text says plainly, "And the men did the work faithfully." That's a good thing to have said about you. I'd settle for "the cookies came out even."
It's actually true. The text says, "And the men did the work faithfully." That's the verdict on the crew repairing the house of the LORD. A good word to earn, friend.

Task by task is the answer. The text says the Levites over the laborers supervised all who did the work, task by task. That's steady attention, not a drive-by. Supervising like that is a lot like watching an oven door, and I would know.

Once a month would be a lot of room for things to go sideways. The text says the Levites over the laborers supervised all who did the work, task by task. That's close, steady oversight. Not a monthly check-in.

The text doesn't say they waited for the end. It says the Levites over the laborers supervised all who did the work, task by task. They were watching the work as it happened. Nobody wants to find out about the burnt batch after it's cooled, friend.

That's right. The text says some of the Levites were secretaries, officers, and gatekeepers. They're the ones who kept the records and the doors in order. It takes all kinds of jobs to run a house, and every one of them is named.

No soldiers or chariots here. The text says some of the Levites were secretaries, officers, and gatekeepers. These Levites worked at the house of the LORD, keeping things running. Those are quieter jobs, but I'd still hire all three.

No fields or flocks in this verse. The text says some of the Levites were secretaries, officers, and gatekeepers. Those are the jobs listed alongside their supervising. Keeping records and guarding doors takes serious focus, friend.
